title: Animals and Plants
description: Ten short stories, reports, letters and diary entries about animals and plants: an animal hospital, a historic glass house, bees on a roof, a dog trainer, a bird walk, an orchid collector, a castle garden, an actress and her adopted dog, an inventor's plant shield and sea turtles at a beach resort.

lessons.title: Rosie at the Animal Hospital
lessons.summary: A dog injures her leg in the park, and a vet treats the cut and warns her owner about a virus.
lessons.text:
Last Saturday morning, I took my dog Rosie to the park, as I do every weekend. I had not noticed that her collar was loose. When Rosie saw a rabbit, she pulled back hard, her head came out of the loose collar, and she ran off into the trees.

By the time I found her, ten minutes later, she was standing on three legs. She had injured her rear leg on an old metal fence, and there was a deep cut just above her foot. I carried her to the car and drove straight to the animal hospital. Even though it was the weekend, it was open.

A nurse took us into a small room, and soon Dr. Lane came in. She is the clinical director of the hospital, which means that she is in charge of the care that every animal receives there. She has more than 20 years of clinical experience.

Dr. Lane looked carefully at the injured leg. She told me that the cut was not as bad as it looked. However, she warned me that a cut from old metal could easily lead to an infection. She cleaned the cut, closed it with a few stitches and gave me some pills to prevent an infection.

Before we left, Dr. Lane asked me whether Rosie had had all her shots. I said I wasn't sure. She warned me that a virus was going around among dogs in our part of the city. She explained that dogs in the park were exposed to the virus every day, because they played and drank water together. A dog that has had its shots usually gets only a light cough, whereas a dog that hasn't can get very sick. Dr. Lane checked her computer and found that Rosie needed one more shot, so she gave it to her right away.

For a week, Rosie stayed at home. Every morning, I checked her rear leg, and every morning it looked better. When we went back, Dr. Lane said there was no sign of infection, and she took out the stitches.

On the way home, I bought Rosie a new collar. It is not loose at all, and I check it every time we go out.

Questions:
Why did Rosie run off in the park?
Her collar was loose, and her head came out of it when she pulled back.
How did Rosie get injured?
She injured her rear leg on an old metal fence.
What does Dr. Lane do at the hospital?
She is the clinical director, so she is in charge of the care that every animal receives there.
What did Dr. Lane warn the writer about?
She warned that a cut from old metal could lead to an infection, and that a virus was going around among dogs.
Why were dogs in the park exposed to the virus?
They were exposed to it because they played and drank water together.
What did the writer buy on the way home?
The writer bought Rosie a new collar that is not loose.

lessons.title: The Glass House Opens Again
lessons.summary: A short news report on a historic glass building in a city garden and its new desert exhibit.
lessons.text:
After two years of repair work, the historic Glass House at the City Garden opened again last Saturday. The building stands on Park Avenue, and it is one of the oldest buildings on the avenue. It was built in 1898, at a time when rich families in the city liked to show off rare plants from other parts of the world.

The Glass House is vast. It is about 100 meters long, and its roof is almost 20 meters high. On a sunny morning, its thousands of glass panels shine like crystal, and people walking along the avenue often stop to take pictures of it.

The repairs were extensive. Workers put in more than 2,000 new panels of glass, repaired the old metal frame and added a modern heating system. "The work was extensive, and it took longer than we had planned," said Helen Ward, the director of the garden. "Nevertheless, we kept every part of the historic building that we could."

Inside, the building has 3 rooms. The first room is warm and wet, like a forest in Central America, whereas the third room is hot and dry, like a desert. This desert room holds the new exhibit that everyone is talking about. The exhibit has more than 300 kinds of desert plants, and some of them can live for a whole year without rain. The plants are surrounded by red rocks and sand, and a painting of a vast desert covers the back wall. In a small glass case in the corner, the exhibit also shows crystals that were found in desert soil.

Many of the plants were imported from other countries. Importing plants is not simple, because each plant must be checked for insects and diseases before it can enter the country. "Some of these plants waited 6 months before we could import them," Ms. Ward said.

The soil is just as important as the plants. Desert plants need soil that dries quickly, because wet soil can kill them. For that reason, the garden made its own soil, using sand, small stones and only a little earth.

Visitors seem to love the new exhibit. "It's like walking through a real desert," said one visitor. The Glass House is open every day except Monday. Tickets cost $8 for adults, and children under 12 enter for free.

Questions:
When was the Glass House built?
It was built in 1898.
Why do people on the avenue stop to take pictures?
They stop because the glass panels shine like crystal on a sunny morning.
What did the extensive repairs include?
Workers put in new glass, repaired the metal frame and added a heating system.
What surrounds the plants in the desert exhibit?
Red rocks and sand surround them.
Why is importing plants not simple?
Each plant must be checked for insects and diseases first.
Why does the garden make its own soil?
Desert plants need soil that dries quickly, because wet soil can kill them.

lessons.title: Bees on the Roof
lessons.summary: A woman keeps two hives on the roof deck of her apartment building and writes about her first summer.
lessons.text:
April 20

Today my two hives arrived, and we put them on the roof deck of our apartment building. The deck gets a lot of sun, and there is a large park across the street, so the bees will have plenty of flowers. My teacher is Mr. Ortiz, who has kept bees for 40 years. He told me that I should stay calm and move slowly. I was fairly nervous, but the bees were fairly calm too.

May 15

Today I went to the monthly meeting of the city bee club. About 30 people came. Mr. Ortiz told us that a hive is a dynamic place. It changes every day: young bees become workers, old bees die, and the number of bees grows quickly in spring. "Because a hive is so dynamic," he said, "you have to look inside it often."

I asked him how much honey my hives would make. He laughed and said that nobody could predict that. He explained that the amount depended on the weather, the flowers and the bees themselves. "If someone tells you they can predict it," he said, "don't believe them."

June 30

My monthly check today went well. Both hives are full of bees. I asked Mr. Ortiz whether there was a formula for good honey. He told me there was no secret formula. "Healthy bees, plenty of flowers and a patient person," he said. "That's the only formula I know."

August 25

Today we took the honey out of the hives. We filled 18 bottles! The family on the third floor helped me, and their children could not wait to taste it. When I gave a bottle to Mrs. Kim, the oldest woman in our building, she said, "Bless you, dear." She told me that her mother used to keep bees and always said that bees were a blessing for any garden.

I felt a lot of pride when I looked at the bottles of golden honey. Of course, the bees are the real honey makers, not me. They do all the work, and I just carry the bottles. Still, I think a little pride is fine.

September 10

At the last monthly meeting, Mr. Ortiz asked me to tell the club about my first summer. I said that the little honey makers on our deck had brought our whole building together. Bless those bees!

Questions:
Where did the writer put her hives?
She put them on the roof deck of her apartment building.
Why did Mr. Ortiz say that a hive is a dynamic place?
He said it because a hive changes every day and grows quickly in spring.
Why can nobody predict how much honey a hive will make?
The amount depends on the weather, the flowers and the bees themselves.
What is Mr. Ortiz's formula for good honey?
His formula is healthy bees, plenty of flowers and a patient person.
What did Mrs. Kim say when she got a bottle of honey?
She said, "Bless you, dear."
Who are the real honey makers?
The bees are the real honey makers.

lessons.title: Pepper Learns to Walk
lessons.summary: A young man and his strong dog take lessons with a trainer, who teaches them to walk calmly together.
lessons.text:
Jake loves his dog, Pepper. She is a big, happy dog, and Jake calls her his best buddy. However, walking with his buddy was not fun. Pepper pulled on the leash all the time. She wanted to go faster than Jake, and when she saw another dog, she jumped and pulled even harder. Several times, the leash twisted around Jake's legs, and once he almost fell.

Jake decided that he had to resolve the problem, so he called a dog trainer named Maria. Initially, Jake thought that Pepper would need a few long lessons. Maria, however, insisted on short lessons. She explained that a dog learns most effectively in short sessions of 5 or 10 minutes. "Long lessons make a dog tired and bored," she said. "Short ones work better."

Maria also insisted on one more thing. She asked Jake to commit to practicing twice a day, every day. "Can you commit to that?" she asked. "There are no exceptions. Not on weekends, and not when it rains." Jake laughed and said he would try. Maria smiled and said, "Don't try. Commit."

The first lesson was about pace. Maria told Jake to walk at a slow, steady pace. Whenever Pepper pulled, Jake had to stop and stand still. As soon as the leash was loose again, he could walk on. Initially, they stopped every few steps. Nevertheless, he did not give up. He made no exceptions: he practiced on weekends, and he practiced in the rain.

After a week, something changed. Pepper began to walk at Jake's pace. When she felt the leash get tight, she looked back at him and waited. Maria said that this was exactly what they wanted, and that they had almost resolved the problem. She explained that Pepper had learned that pulling did not get her anywhere, whereas walking calmly did.

Jake asked Maria about other dogs. She told him that other dogs would be the hardest part. They practiced near the park, at a safe distance from other dogs at first. Each time Pepper stayed calm, Jake gave her a treat.

Today, two months later, Jake and Pepper walk through the park every evening at a relaxed pace. The problem is resolved. The leash never twists around Jake's legs anymore. Pepper is still his best buddy, and now walking with her is the best part of his day.

Questions:
What was the problem with walking Pepper?
Pepper pulled on the leash all the time, and the leash twisted around Jake's legs.
Why did Maria insist on short lessons?
She said a dog learns most effectively in short sessions of 5 or 10 minutes.
What did Jake have to commit to?
He had to commit to practicing twice a day, with no exceptions.
What did Jake do whenever Pepper pulled?
He stopped and stood still until the leash was loose again.
What had Pepper learned after a week?
She had learned that pulling did not get her anywhere, whereas walking calmly did.
How do Jake and Pepper walk now?
They walk through the park every evening at a relaxed pace.

lessons.title: The Spring Bird Walk
lessons.summary: A bird-watching club's newsletter reports on its spring walk by the lake and invites new members.
lessons.text:
Dear members,

Our spring bird walk took place last Sunday, and it was one of the best walks we have had in years. In spite of the cold wind, 22 participants came, which is a new record for our club. The youngest participant was 8 years old, and the oldest was 84.

We met at the north end of Mill Lake at 7 in the morning and followed the 5-kilometer path around the lake. A 5-kilometer walk sounds long, but we walked at a slow pace and stopped often, so nobody got tired.

The main reason for this walk is always the arrival of the spring birds. Every year, thousands of birds return from the south in April, and their arrival is a sure sign that winter is over. This year, we did not have to wait long. Near the parking lot, we saw a robin with a bright orange breast hopping across the grass. A few minutes later, a small brown bird hopped along a branch right above our heads, singing loudly. Several participants saw a woodpecker for the first time.

The high point of the morning came at the east end of the lake, where a hawk was sitting in a tall tree. A hawk is a skilled hunter. It can see a mouse from very high in the air. As we watched, the hunter flew down to the grass, caught something small and flew back to its tree. Its feathers were brown, with a light breast and a jet-black head. Nobody in the group made a sound. Then a jet flew low over the lake, and the hawk flew away.

After the walk, we had hot coffee and cookies at the visitor center. In total, the group counted 41 kinds of birds.

If you saw a bird that we did not list, please add it to our online forum. On the forum, you will also find a map of the lake where you can put a pin for each bird you saw. Many members have already added their pins, and the map looks great.

Finally, a reminder about membership. Membership costs $15 a year, or $5 for students. Every new member receives a small club pin in the shape of a bird. If your membership ends this month, you can renew it on the forum. See you at the next walk!

Questions:
How many participants came to the spring walk?
22 participants came, which is a new record for the club.
How long was the path around the lake?
It was 5 kilometers long.
What is the arrival of the spring birds a sign of?
It is a sure sign that winter is over.
What did the group see near the parking lot?
They saw a robin with an orange breast hopping across the grass.
Why is a hawk a skilled hunter?
It can see a mouse from very high in the air.
What can members do on the forum?
They can add birds to the list and put a pin on the map for each bird they saw.

lessons.title: A Life with Orchids
lessons.summary: A newspaper profile of a retired teacher who collects orchids and wins a prize at a flower show.
lessons.text:
Many people believe that collecting orchids is a hobby for people with great wealth. Ruth Allen, who is 76 years old and lives in a small house on Hill Street, does not agree. "You don't need wealth to collect orchids," she says. "You need patience and passion."

Ruth's passion for orchids began when she was 10 years old. Her father, a quiet man who worked at the post office, was a great plant lover. One day he brought home a small orchid with white flowers and gave it to her. "I owe my passion to my father," Ruth says. "I owe him a lot of things, but this is the most important one."

Today, Ruth has more than 200 orchids. They fill the shelves of a small glass room behind her house. Some of them are very rare, but most of them were not expensive at all. Ruth explains that she buys small, young plants, because they cost much less than big ones. Then she waits, sometimes for years, until they produce flowers.

Not every plant survives. When an orchid dies, Ruth does not buy a replacement right away. First, she tries to understand what went wrong. Was there too much water? Too little light? "A replacement is easy to buy," she says. "Learning from the mistake is much more useful."

For 30 years, Ruth taught science at the local high school. She has also written a short book entitled Orchids for Beginners, and she gives talks to other plant lovers at the library. Her most popular talk is entitled "The Patient Gardener."

Last month, Ruth took one of her orchids to the state flower show. A jury of 5 experts looked at more than 400 plants. The jury spent a long time in front of Ruth's orchid, which had 12 perfect pink flowers. In the end, the jury said that it was the most outstanding plant of the show. They explained that its flowers were superior to all the others in color and in shape.

At the prize ceremony, Ruth thanked the jury and the other plant lovers. Then she spoke about her father. After the ceremony, many young people came to ask her for advice. "That was the best prize of all," she says.

Questions:
What does Ruth say you need to collect orchids?
She says you need patience and passion, not wealth.
Who does Ruth owe her passion to?
She owes her passion to her father, who was a great plant lover.
What does Ruth do before she buys a replacement for a dead plant?
First, she tries to understand what went wrong.
What is Ruth's book entitled?
It is entitled Orchids for Beginners.
What did the jury say about Ruth's orchid?
The jury said that it was the most outstanding plant of the show and that its flowers were superior to all the others.
What happened after the ceremony?
Many young people came to ask Ruth for advice.

lessons.title: The Garden of Elton Castle
lessons.summary: On a trip, a visitor tours an old castle's gardens and hears the tale of a knight who planted roses.
lessons.text:
Last summer, my husband and I spent a week in England. The best day of our trip was the day we visited Elton Castle. The castle is more than 700 years old, and it stands on a hill above a slow, quiet river. Today, most visitors come for its gardens rather than its walls.

Our guide, a young woman named Beth, began the tour at the river. She showed us a place where the water was only knee-deep. She explained that in the past, before there were bridges, people crossed the river at this shallow place, which is called a ford. Farmers, horses and soldiers all crossed at the ford. The river was also the boundary of the castle's land. Everything on our side of the boundary belonged to the castle.

Then we walked up the hill and through the main gate. Inside the outer walls, there are large gardens with fruit trees and vegetables. Behind a second, smaller wall is the inner garden. Beth told us that the inner garden was the oldest part of the gardens and that, for hundreds of years, only the family and its guests could enter it.

In the inner garden, Beth told us a tale that people in the area still tell their children. A long time ago, a young knight lived in the castle. He had to leave home to fight in a war far away. Before he left, he promised his wife that he would come home and plant a garden for her. The war lasted 7 years. When the knight finally came home, he kept his promise. He planted a rose garden in the inner garden, and the red rose became the symbol of the family. Even today, the red rose is the symbol on the castle's flag.

In the corner of the inner garden, there is also a small garden of herbs. Beth explained that the castle once had its own priest. The priest grew herbs for cooking and for medicine, and he helped people from the nearby village when they were sick.

Beth said that nobody knew whether the tale of the knight was true. Nevertheless, the roses are real, and they smell wonderful. We sat on a bench in the inner garden for a long time before we left the castle.

Questions:
What is a ford?
A ford is a shallow place in a river where people can walk across.
What was the river the boundary of?
It was the boundary of the castle's land.
Who could enter the inner garden in the past?
Only the family and its guests could enter it.
What did the knight promise his wife?
He promised that he would come home and plant a garden for her.
What became the symbol of the family?
The red rose became the symbol of the family.
What did the priest grow in the inner garden?
He grew herbs for cooking and for medicine.

lessons.title: A Star and an Old Dog
lessons.summary: A reporter's column about a famous actress who adopted an old dog from a shelter.
lessons.text:
In my 15 years as a reporter, I have met many celebrities. Most of them want to talk about their new movie or their new song. When the actress Grace Miller called the newspaper last month, I expected the same thing. Instead, she wanted to talk about a dog.

"I'd like to invite you to the city animal shelter on Saturday," she said. "I want to show you something." It's not every day that a celebrity asks a reporter to visit an animal shelter, so I said yes.

On Saturday morning, the actress met me at the door. She was wearing old jeans and a simple sweater, and nobody at the shelter seemed to treat her like a celebrity. She told me that she had volunteered there every Saturday for 3 years. She walks the dogs, cleans the cages and plays with the cats.

Then she introduced me to Duke, a 12-year-old dog with a white face and sad brown eyes. Duke had lived at the shelter for almost a year. Most people want young dogs, so the old ones often wait the longest. Grace told me that she had adopted Duke the week before. That Saturday, she was taking him home. She explained that she had decided to tell the newspaper because she wanted more people to think about old animals. "An old dog is calm, quiet and grateful," she said.

A week later, Grace was kind enough to invite me to her house. Duke was sleeping on the sofa. She told me that she reads her scripts out loud to him when she learns a new role. "He's the best listener," she said, laughing. "He never complains about a bad script."

While I was writing this column, I kept asking myself why her story touched me so much. I think that the love between people and animals is universal. It doesn't matter whether you are a famous actress or a reporter. A dog doesn't know who you are, and it doesn't care. It just wants someone to love. That feeling is universal, and it is the reason this column is about Duke and not about a movie.

If you have room in your home, the shelter has 14 older dogs waiting to be adopted.

Questions:
What did the reporter expect when the actress called?
The reporter expected her to talk about a new movie.
Where did Grace invite the reporter to go?
She invited the reporter to the city animal shelter.
What does Grace do at the shelter every Saturday?
She walks the dogs, cleans the cages and plays with the cats.
Why did Grace tell the newspaper that she had adopted Duke?
She wanted more people to think about old animals.
What does Grace read to Duke?
She reads her scripts to him when she learns a new role.
What does the reporter think is universal?
The reporter thinks that the love between people and animals is universal.

lessons.title: The Plant Shield
lessons.summary: An engineer invents a cover that shields young plants, gets a patent and starts a company with an investor.
lessons.text:
For 12 years, Dana Brooks worked as an engineer at an auto factory outside the city. She designed parts for car doors. It was a good job with a good salary, and she was good at it. In her free time, however, Dana had a different passion: her vegetable garden.

Every spring, Dana faced the same problem. When she planted young plants outside, cold nights and strong winds often killed them. She tried plastic bags and old bottles, but nothing worked well. One evening, she had an idea. She would design a light, clear cover that could shield each young plant from the wind and the cold, while still letting in the sun.

Dana used the skills she had learned at the auto factory. She did a lot of math to find the best shape and size, and she made her first shield from clear plastic. The next spring, she put 20 shields in her garden. Every plant under a shield survived, whereas half of the plants without a shield died.

Dana knew she had a good idea, so she applied for a patent. A patent is a legal document which says that nobody else can make or sell your invention without your permission. After 18 months, she received the patent.

Now she needed money to make the shields. She met with several investors. The first investors were not interested, but the fourth investor, a woman named Rosa Diaz, loved the idea. Rosa agreed to give Dana $200,000. In return, she would own part of the company.

Dana left her job at the auto factory. It was not easy to give up a steady salary, but she decided to take the risk. She and Rosa incorporated a new company called Green Shield. Dana also incorporated a few new ideas into the design. For example, she added small holes so that the air could move.

Rosa helped Dana make a careful business plan, and then they had to execute it. They executed the plan step by step: first a small factory, then a website, then garden stores. In the first year, sales were slow. In the second year, sales rocketed after the shield appeared on a TV gardening show. That year, the company's gross sales were more than $2 million.

Dana still does the math for every new design herself. "I'm an engineer," she says. "I love the math."

Questions:
Where did Dana work before she started her company?
She worked as an engineer at an auto factory, where she had a good salary.
What does the plant shield do?
It shields young plants from the wind and the cold, while still letting in the sun.
What is a patent?
It is a legal document which says that nobody else can make or sell your invention without permission.
Who was the investor that helped Dana?
The investor was Rosa Diaz, who gave Dana $200,000.
Why did sales rocket in the second year?
They rocketed after the shield appeared on a TV gardening show.
What were the company's gross sales that year?
They were more than $2 million.

lessons.title: Turtle Nights
lessons.summary: In an e-mail, a woman tells her friend about a beach resort that protects sea turtles and their eggs.
lessons.text:
Hi Sarah,

We're back from our week in Florida, and I have to tell you about it! I'm sending you some pics, so you can see everything I describe.

We stayed at a small resort on a vast, quiet beach. The first pic shows the view from our room: just sand and ocean, as far as you can see. On our first evening, the manager of the resort explained that the beach is a special place for sea turtles. Between May and October, female turtles come out of the ocean at night to deposit their eggs in the sand. Each turtle makes a hole, deposits about 100 eggs in it and then returns to the sea.

Because of the turtles, the resort follows some clear rules. After 9 in the evening, all the lights near the beach are turned off. The manager explained that baby turtles find the ocean by following the light of the moon on the water. If there are bright lights on the beach, the babies go the wrong way.

The resort also stopped its weekly fireworks show. The loud bang of the fireworks scared the turtles, and some of them returned to the sea without depositing their eggs. A few guests were opposed to the new rules, because they had always loved the fireworks. However, most guests were not opposed at all. The manager told us that it was a small sacrifice for the guests and a big help for the turtles. I agree. Giving up the fireworks is not a real sacrifice when you think about what you get instead.

On our fourth night, we joined a walk with a turtle guide. We walked in the dark for an hour. We barely spoke, and nobody dared to use a phone. Then we saw a huge turtle slowly making a hole in the sand. Nobody dared to move until she had finished and gone back into the water. There's no pic of her, of course, because cameras weren't allowed.

Two nights later, we saw baby turtles coming out of a nest. They were barely bigger than a coin, and they ran straight to the water. Without a single bang or bright light, they found the ocean all by themselves.

I'd love to go back next year. Maybe you can come too!

Love,
Kate

Questions:
Where did Kate stay in Florida?
She stayed at a small resort on a vast, quiet beach.
Why do female turtles come out of the ocean at night?
They come out to deposit their eggs in the sand.
Why are the lights near the beach turned off?
Baby turtles find the ocean by following the moon, and bright lights make them go the wrong way.
Why did the resort stop its fireworks show?
The loud bang scared the turtles.
Why were some guests opposed to the new rules?
They were opposed because they had always loved the fireworks.
How big were the baby turtles?
They were barely bigger than a coin.
